sents.text: By some estimates, half the nitrogen in your body was pulled from the air by a machine.
Not a plant.
A machine.
The air is seventy-eight percent nitrogen.
Every cell needs it.
For most of history, we couldn't use a breath of it.
Three men cracked that problem.
Only two became famous.
And the same chemistry that fed billions would also fuel a war.
In 1898, the British scientist Sir William Crookes used his presidential address to the British Association to deliver a warning.
The world, he said, was heading toward a wheat shortage.
Populations were rising.
Farmland was wearing out.
And the thing crops needed most was running low.
That thing was nitrogen.
Plants can't use nitrogen gas.
Its two atoms are bound so tightly that only a few things in nature can pull them apart — certain bacteria, and the violence of lightning.
Everything else has to be recycled: manure, compost, the remains of living things.
By the nineteenth century, recycling wasn't enough.
So the world went looking for nitrogen that was already fixed — and found it in two strange places.
The first was bird droppings: centuries of seabird guano, piled on islands off the coast of Peru and shipped to Europe by the ton.
The second was the Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth, where vast beds of sodium nitrate lay just beneath the surface.
But in the 1870s, the richest of those deposits were not in Chile.
They lay in Peru's southern province of Tarapacá, and along Bolivia's coast, around the port of Antofagasta.
Much of the work there was done by Chilean and British companies.
In 1878, Bolivia tried to raise taxes on the Chilean-run Antofagasta Nitrate Company.
When Bolivia threatened to seize the company's property, Chilean forces occupied Antofagasta on February fourteenth, eighteen seventy-nine.
Bolivia declared war on Chile — and Chile went to war with both Bolivia and its ally, Peru.
It became known as the War of the Pacific.
It lasted five years.
Chile won.
In the Treaty of Ancón, in 1883, Peru gave up Tarapacá.
A truce in 1884 gave Chile the entire Bolivian coast, with its nitrate, copper and mineral industries.
A treaty in 1904 made it permanent.
Bolivia has had no coastline... ever since.
Chilean saltpeter became one of the world's most sought-after commodities.
And here's the problem.
Nitrate didn't only grow wheat.
It also made gunpowder and explosives.
Whoever controlled those sea lanes controlled both food and firepower.
Crookes's message was simple: the deposits would not last.
The way forward was to take nitrogen straight from the air.
Someone had to figure out how.
Fritz Haber was a chemist at the technical university in Karlsruhe, Germany — ambitious, brilliant, and restless.
He had begun studying the reaction that mattered: nitrogen plus hydrogen, making ammonia.
Haber had grown up in Breslau, then a German city, today Wrocław in Poland, in a Jewish family.
He was proud, driven, and fiercely loyal to Germany.
In 1901, he married another chemist from Breslau: Clara Immerwahr.
Just months earlier, in December 1900, Clara had become the first woman to earn a doctorate from the University of Breslau.
She defended her thesis in the university's main hall — and many young women of the city came to watch.
After the wedding, the expectations of the time left her little room for her own research.
Her husband's career came first.
Remember her name.
In Part 2, she becomes part of the story.
On paper, Haber's reaction is simple.
In practice, it's a trap.
Heat the gases, and the reaction speeds up — but the ammonia falls apart again.
Cool them down, and almost nothing happens at all.
Haber's early measurements found only tiny traces of ammonia.
And in May 1907, at a meeting of the Bunsen Society in Hamburg, Walther Nernst — one of the most respected chemists in Germany — publicly called Haber's numbers very inaccurate.
Haber was deeply offended.
But Nernst had also proposed repeating the measurements at higher pressure.
Haber took that idea further than anyone had dared.
To do it, he needed someone who could build equipment that didn't yet exist.
That person was Robert Le Rossignol — a young British chemist from the island of Jersey, trained at University College London, who had joined Haber in Karlsruhe.
Le Rossignol built the high-pressure apparatus — with valves and seals that could hold gas at around two hundred times normal atmospheric pressure.
Near the end of his life, he summed up their partnership simply: Haber did the theoretical side, and he did the engineering side.
Their apparatus kept circulating the unreacted gas over a catalyst, drawing off ammonia as it formed.
The rare metal osmium made it work.
By the summer of 1909, they were ready to show it to the people who could make it real.
Since 1908, Haber had been working under contract with BASF — the Badische Anilin- und Soda-Fabrik, one of the largest chemical companies in the world.
On July 2nd, 1909, Haber and Le Rossignol invited BASF to Karlsruhe for a demonstration.
Carl Bosch was invited.
But it was the chemist Alwin Mittasch and the company's chief mechanic, Julius Kranz, who watched.
What they saw was a machine that sat on a table.
And out of it, drop by drop, came liquid ammonia — made from the air.
Roughly two cubic centimeters a minute, hour after hour.
It wasn't much.
But it was continuous.
It didn't stop.
Le Rossignol kept a sealed glass tube of the ammonia made that day.
More than forty years later, he gave it to the Science Museum in London.
The next day, Haber sent BASF's directors a report of what they had witnessed.
But a machine on a table is not a factory.
And there was a question that still hangs over this moment: whose invention was it?
The process would be called the Haber process.
Later, the Haber-Bosch process.
But look closely... at the paperwork.
On the American patent, Haber put Le Rossignol's name beside his own — and gave him a share of the royalties that would one day make him rich.
Le Rossignol later said that Haber had handled the whole patent matter.
He left Karlsruhe in August 1909, just as BASF began the long work of industrialization.
He went on to a career in industrial research in Britain, and used his royalty income for philanthropy.
The Nobel Prize, when it came, went to Haber alone.
Le Rossignol's name faded from the story.
So here's a question for you.
Who deserves the credit for an invention — the person with the idea, the person who builds the first working machine, or the person who makes it work for millions?
Tell us what you think in the comments.
And the second name on the process belonged to a man who hadn't built the tabletop machine at all.
He was the one who had to make it work at a scale no one had ever attempted.
Carl Bosch was a BASF chemist with an engineer's mind and training in metallurgy.
In 1909, BASF gave him the job of turning a laboratory experiment into an industry.
The pressures and temperatures it required went well beyond anything industry had handled before.
Three problems stood in the way.
The first was the catalyst.
Osmium worked — but it was extremely rare.
There wasn't enough of it to supply an industry.
So the BASF laboratory under Alwin Mittasch began a systematic search — testing one material after another in small test reactors.
Bosch later said that, over the years, the number of tests grew to... twenty thousand.
The answer was a catalyst based on iron, with small additions of other compounds: cheap, abundant, and durable.
Iron-based catalysts are still used today.
The second problem was more dangerous.
Bosch's team had ordered strong steel reactor tubes from the Mannesmann works.
The first two ran for eighty hours... Then they burst.
When Bosch examined the metal, the inner wall had lost all its elasticity.
As he explained in his Nobel lecture, hydrogen had penetrated the steel and turned it brittle.
Bosch, who knew metallurgy, found the mechanism: the hot, high-pressure hydrogen was pulling carbon out of the steel, leaving it soft and brittle at the same time.
His solution was elegant.
A thin lining of soft steel, inside a strong outer steel jacket drilled with many small holes.
Hydrogen that seeped through the lining could escape through the holes before it weakened the jacket.
The lining could simply be replaced.
The third problem was everything else: making hydrogen and nitrogen cheaply and pure enough, compressing them, and building equipment that could run around the clock.
Hydrogen alone required a new industry.
BASF would make it from coal, coke, air and water — in what Bosch later called the largest gas production facilities ever built.
It took years and enormous risk.
But Bosch's team made high-pressure chemistry work at industrial scale.
That achievement would later earn Bosch his own Nobel Prize, in 1931.
On September 9th, 1913, the world's first ammonia synthesis plant went into operation at Oppau — today part of Ludwigshafen, on the Rhine.
According to BASF, the new plant could produce up to... thirty tonnes of ammonia a day.
Nobody yet knew exactly how farmers' crops would respond to this new fertilizer.
So in the spring of 1914, on Bosch's proposal, BASF set up an agricultural research station at Limburgerhof, near Ludwigshafen, to find out.
What started as drops on a tabletop became one of the most important industrial processes ever created.
Synthetic fertilizer spread across the world through the twentieth century, helping farmers grow far more food on the same land.
Researchers estimate that by the early twenty-first century, close to... half of the world's population was being fed by food grown with nitrogen from this process.
Crookes's famine never came the way he feared.
The chemists had pulled bread out of the air.
But remember what else nitrate made.
Germany had no nitrate deposits of its own.
Most of what it used — for its fields, and for its explosives — came by sea, from Chile.
In the summer of 1914, Europe went to war.
And the sea lanes were about to close.
Robert Le Rossignol, the British engineer who had built the first machine, was still living in Germany.
When war broke out, he was interned as an enemy alien — and later released to work for a German company for the rest of the war.
